source.title: Rethinking the Role of Efficient Attention in Hybrid Architectures
source.authors: Zi-Qing Qiao; Yi-Nuo Xu; Chao-Jun Xiao; Zhou Su; Zi-Han Zhou; Yingfa Chen; Xiao-Yue Xu; Xu Han; Zhi-Yuan Liu

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study fits power-law scaling curves to held-out validation loss across model sizes and training-token budgets, and checks fits against held-out and larger-scale runs. It applies a scaling-law measurement to new hybrid architectures.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports mechanistic and downstream-benchmark experiments, but those do not test whether downstream performance is predictable from scale or pretraining loss. The LongPPL findings are included as related results but use a long-context proxy rather than held-out pretraining cross-entropy. Cited scaling-law results from other studies are not recorded as findings here.
record.test_reason: The study fits L(N,D)=aN^-α+bD^-β to held-out C4 validation loss over S1–S3 (15M–65M non-embedding parameters, D=100N–1000N). It verifies the fits on held-out S4 (104M) and S5 (0.48B) runs for ten matched-size architectures. This is the original measure with a near-original fitting method, so T1, in a new setting of hybrid attention architectures. The fits are tools for comparing architectures, but they report fit quality and extrapolation directly, so they bear on V1, V2 and V4.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right but incomplete. Validation loss is well fit by the scaling law and is nearly unaffected by efficient-attention design. The design mainly changes how fast long-context capability (log LongPPL) emerges, and hybrids converge under sufficient training. Mechanistically, full attention carries long-range retrieval and efficient attention acts as an optimization prior ('Large-Window Laziness'). Small-window SWA plus NoPE on the full-attention layers improves long-context performance.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a separable power-law fit to held-out validation loss over parameter and token scales, with held-out and larger-scale checks. It does not test compute-optimal allocation; it also fits log(LongPPL), a distinct long-context proxy.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper excludes the S1 checkpoint at D = 100N from log(LongPPL) fitting because its long-context behavior is unstable. It reports that long-context curves differ across attention designs and training budgets; validation-loss curves overlap closely.

fits_no_version.finding: log(LongPPL) on GovReport key tokens follows the same separable power law, with held-out S4 R² 0.906–0.986.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Long-context perplexity of hybrid LMs scales as a separable power law in N and D.

fits_no_version.finding: Unlike C4 loss, log(LongPPL) differs strongly across efficient-attention designs at low data, especially SWA-2048. The gaps shrink with more training, and the layer ratio, head-wise mixing and NoPE change log(LongPPL) while leaving loss nearly unchanged.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architecture choices that barely affect pretraining loss can strongly affect how fast long-context capability emerges.

fits_no_version.finding: The GDN short conv gives a LongPPL advantage at small budgets that reverses at D≥500N.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Effects of auxiliary mixer components on long-context perplexity depend on training budget.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The authors note that the largest model remains sub-billion parameter scale, training reaches at most approximately 100B tokens, and the models are pretrained directly at 16K context before extension to at most 32K. Some fit values and S5 comparisons are shown only in figures, and the text provides no numeric extrapolation-error measure or uncertainty intervals.

untested.parts: Compute scaling. Parameter range over several orders of magnitude: S1–S4 non-embedding N spans about 7x, and S5 reaches about 32x S1. The fit form has no irreducible-loss term.
Extrapolation by orders of magnitude: tested only to S4 (1.6x the largest fit size) and S5 (about 7x).
Depth, width and aspect-ratio sweeps. Only the attention-mixer type and a few hybrid design choices are varied, at matched parameter counts.
Downstream benchmarks are reported for three models only, with no predictive relation to scale or loss.
No variation of fitting method, schedule or parameter counting. Curvature away from a power law is not examined.

missing.what: Predicted S5 (0.48B) validation-loss curves of all seven architectures closely overlap Full across all D. This is the main cross-architecture evidence for V4 and is figure-only.
Fit R² for the three design variants: SWA-128(1:3) 0.995/0.981, Headwise 0.998/0.963, NoPE 0.997/0.968.
GDN with expand_v=1 consistently beats dv>dk on validation loss; qualitative, with no numbers.

record.verdict_notes: Rows were tagged with V4 even though they report fit R². V4 evidence should rest on the loss-overlap comparisons, which are mostly qualitative or figure-only. The reader's V2 limits_scope label was dropped: the lack of an orders-of-magnitude test is an untested part, not a qualification. All models are sub-billion scale with at most about 100B tokens, pretrained at 16K context on a long/short data mix, with a WSD schedule rerun per budget. The fit form omits an irreducible-loss term. No uncertainty intervals are reported.

versions.untested_parts: Compute scaling is not tested; the paper fits loss against parameters and training tokens.
The tested extrapolation is limited to the paper's S4/S5 scales and its stated training budgets, not runs orders of magnitude larger.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token split is reported.
The comparisons cover the tested hybrid-attention choices and design variants, not a broad sweep of depth, width, and architecture choices.
No other modality or training regime is tested.
Downstream benchmarks are reported, but no predictive relation to pretraining loss or scale is fitted or evaluated.
The study does not vary fitting methods or setup choices to test exponent or compute-optimal-split dependence, and does not report systematic bending away from a power law.
